bib.title: Scaling Transformer to 1M tokens and beyond with RMT

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Scaling Transformer to 1M tokens and beyond with RMT", Aydar Bulatov, Yuri Kuratov, Yermek Kapushev, Mikhail Burtsev. The PDF carries an AAAI 2024 copyright line and "arXiv:2304.11062v2 [cs.CL] 6 Feb 2024", so it is the AAAI 2024 version of a 2023 arXiv paper. The paper never says "AAAI 2024 proceedings" outright.

COVERAGE: All 48,938 chars were read: the body, the Limitations section, and Appendix A (efficiency, task generation, curriculum, parameter-efficient methods, Table 1). I only skimmed the references. Figures 5, 7, 9, 11 and 12 report their results as plots, so the extraction has no accuracy numbers for them. I did not view the images. I also read the target note. It does not cite this paper (its sources list has no Bulatov).

CLAIMS (ranked)
- claim: The authors extend a pretrained BERT with recurrent memory tokens (RMT) and report it uses memory on synthetic fact tasks up to 2M tokens, with linear compute and constant memory.
  number: 4,096 segments, 2,048,000 tokens (2,043,904 in the text)
  setup: BERT backbone, 512-token segments (499 usable, 10 memory tokens, 3 special tokens), trained on at most 7 segments with curriculum, evaluated up to 4,096 segments. Tasks are synthetic bAbI facts in QuALITY filler: Memorize, Detect & Memorize, and two-fact Reasoning. No accuracy figure is given in the text.
  quote: "During inference, the model effectively utilized memory for up to 4,096 segments with a total length of 2,048,000 tokens"
  where: Fig. 5 caption, p. 5. The text also says "we increase the validation task size up to 4096 segments or 2,043,904 tokens". Detect & Memorize is the easiest and Reasoning the hardest.
- claim: With a fixed 512-token segment, RMT's FLOPs grow linearly with input length. Full-attention OPT models drift toward quadratic scaling on long inputs.
  number: x29 fewer FLOPs than OPT-175B and x295 fewer than OPT-125M (printed as "OPT-135M") at 2,048,000 tokens
  setup: Analytic FLOP estimate, not a measured run. It uses OPT configs and the FLOP formulas of Hoffmann et al. 2022, adjusted for recurrence, compared against 512-token inputs.
  quote: "On sequences with 2,048,000 tokens, RMT can run OPT-175B with ×29 fewer FLOPs and with ×295 fewer FLOPs than OPT-135M."
  where: Fig. 2 caption, p. 3
- claim: Large models look near-linear below about 32K tokens because feed-forward layers dominate. Past 32K they fall back to quadratic scaling. Small models are quadratic even at short lengths.
  number: 32,000 tokens
  setup: Same FLOP estimate as above.
  quote: "Larger Transformer models tend to exhibit slower quadratic scaling with respect to sequence length because of compute-heavy FFN layers (which scale quadratically with respect to hidden size). However, on extremely long sequences > 32,000, they fall back to quadratic scaling."
  where: p. 3
- claim: Measured memory limit of full attention. GPT-2 runs out of memory at 8K tokens on an 80GB GPU, while RMT's inference memory stays constant because only one segment is in GPU memory at a time.
  number: 8,000 tokens
  setup: Single A100 80GB, HuggingFace GPT-2 (110M) without FlashAttention, FP32, BPTT unroll not limited. This is a deliberately unoptimized baseline, so the OOM point is not a general limit.
  quote: "GPT-2 (110M) OOMs on an 80Gb GPU with 8k tokens."
  where: Fig. 10 caption and appendix, p. 9. Also: "Baseline transformer fails to process sequences with length 8000 with out-of-memory error."
- claim: Related long-context methods hit length or memory ceilings. Sparse or local-attention models were reported under 33K tokens. CoLT5 reached 64K and then ran out of GPU memory.
  number: under 33,000 tokens; CoLT5 64,000
  setup: Figures are from those papers as cited in this one, not re-measured.
  quote: "The longest Longformer, Big Bird, and Long T5 (Guo et al. 2022), LongNet (Ding et al. 2023) models reported in their respective papers have a maximum length of less than 33,000 tokens."
  where: Related Work, p. 2. Next to it: "memory requirements grow with input size during both training and inference, inevitably limiting input scaling due to hardware constraints."
- claim: Context windows of deployed models in 2023, as stated by the authors and now dated.
  number: 32K for GPT-4, 100K for Claude, 64K for CoLT5
  setup: Stated in a figure caption, as of early 2023.
  quote: "significantly exceeding the largest input size reported for transformer models (64K tokens for CoLT5 (Ainslie et al. 2023), and 32K tokens for GPT-4 (OpenAI 2023), and 100K tokens for Claude)"
  where: Fig. 5 caption
- claim: In language modeling, more effective context lowers perplexity. RMT also removes the high loss on the first tokens of a segment, because memory carries information from the previous segment.
  number: none in the text (results are plots in Figs. 7 and 8)
  setup: GPT-2 with 2 memory tokens, trained on ArXiv from The Pile with curriculum. Perplexity is computed on the last target segment only.
  quote: "On the other hand, RMT ensures equally good prediction for all tokens due to carryover of information from the previous segment."
  where: p. 6, Fig. 8. The exact previous context (128 or 768 tokens) gives larger loss gains "but at a higher inference cost".
- claim: Full attention is an upper bound on RMT, because RMT sees only compressed memory states and not the exact past hidden states. This concession matters for the "finite context" argument.
  number: none
  setup: Authors' discussion, not tested.
  quote: "with unlimited resources and general-purpose information to remember, full attention models might still have an edge in performance. We can think of full-attention models as an upper bound for RMT, since RMT has to operate only on memory states that represent compressed information, not on actual exact hidden states of the past."
  where: Limitations and Discussion, p. 8
- claim: Curriculum is essential. Without it, RMT trained straight on 4 segments neither solves the task nor extrapolates. After training on 5 or more segments, it generalizes nearly perfectly to tasks twice as long.
  number: 5 or more training segments; 2x length
  setup: Memorization task, BERT. Fig. 11 gives no numbers in the text.
  quote: "After being trained on 5 or more segments, RMT can generalize nearly perfectly for tasks twice as long."
  where: p. 5. Appendix: "in the absence of the curriculum ... RMT does not learn neither to solve the task, nor to extrapolate on other sequence length."
- claim: Theorem-proving test (Lean/Mathlib lemma memorization) gave only a modest gain.
  number: none in the text
  setup: GPT-Neo 1.3B, 10 memory tokens, segment size "2028" as printed (probably 2048). Compared against GPT-Neo without memory on 2 segments.
  quote: "However, training with 4 or more segments does not enhance predictions for longer sequences."
  where: p. 7. The authors guess the model mostly memorizes the start of the last lemma and that the effect of finding relevant lemmas is "less notable".
- claim: RMT combines with LoRA and adapters.
  number: Pythia-70m loss 41.43 for adapter only; 10.31 for adapter + RMT (1 segment); 7.30 with LoRA added; 6.97 with 2 segments
  setup: ArXiv language modeling, Pythia-70m. The table column is labelled "LOSS" although the text says perplexity. The metric is ambiguous, and 41.43 looks like perplexity.
  quote: "ADAPTER ONLY 41.43 / ADAPTER + RMT-1 SEG 10.31 / ADAPTER + LORA + RMT-1 SEG 7.30 / ADAPTER + LORA + RMT-2 SEG 6.97"
  where: Table 1, p. 9

LIMITS
- The 2M-token result is on synthetic fact-retrieval tasks only. The authors say: "We demonstrate scaling to extremely long sequences such as 2M tokens only on specialized tasks. Unfortunately, there are currently no established benchmarks for NLP tasks with such lengths."
- The distractor text comes from a different distribution than the facts, so the task is easy: "This makes distinguishing questions trivial for the model."
- The paper reports no comparison against full-attention long-context models at long lengths.
- The tests are single-fact and two-fact lookups. The paper does not test aggregation over many lines, so it says nothing about the dense-dependency tasks (OOLONG-style) that the note discusses.
- BPTT cost is still large. Larger models cost more to train, and some tasks may need more segments.
- Memory is lossy compression. This fits the note's theme that compressing context loses information.
- The "no technical limitations" claim for scaling further is an assertion, not a test.
- The backbones are small and old (BERT, GPT-2, GPT-Neo 1.3B, Pythia-70m). No modern LLM is tested.
- The FLOP comparison is analytic. The only measured efficiency run is one unoptimized GPT-2 FP32 test.
- The context sizes of GPT-4 and Claude are dated.

BUILDS ON: Bulatov, Kuratov and Burtsev 2022, Recurrent Memory Transformer (NeurIPS 35). Memory Transformer (Burtsev et al. 2020) supplies the memory-token idea. Transformer-XL (Dai et al. 2019), Compressive Transformer (Rae et al. 2020), Memformer (Wu et al. 2022a) and Block-Recurrent Transformer (Hutchins et al. 2022) are cited as recurrent-segment predecessors. bAbI (Weston et al. 2016) and QuALITY (Pang et al. 2022) supply the task data. FLOP counting follows Hoffmann et al. 2022. It cites Liu et al. 2023 (Lost in the middle) as motivation.

CODE: none in the paper (it points to github.com/booydar/t5-experiments/tree/aaai24). The recurrence is given as equations: memory tokens are prepended to the segment, the transformer runs, and the output memory tokens become the next segment's input memory.

FIGURES (not viewed; captions from the extraction)
- Fig. 1, p. 2: recurrent memory mechanism. Memory is passed along with the segment embeddings.
- Fig. 2, p. 3: log-log FLOP scaling of RMT vs OPT models from 512 to 2,048,000 tokens. This is the quickest way to see linear vs quadratic.
- Fig. 5, p. 5: accuracy vs length out to 2M for the three tasks.
- Fig. 10, p. 9: GPU memory and iteration time vs input size, showing the GPT-2 OOM at 8K.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions. The extraction is clean text, except that figure data are plots and not text. Typos in the source: "OPT-135M" for OPT-125M, "2028" segment size, and Table 1 labelled LOSS where the text says perplexity.
